drill.title: Calibrate a thermometer in ice water
body: Every safe-temperature check this year depends on your thermometer reading correctly. A mixture of ice and water sits at 32°F, which makes it a reliable reference point.
The second part is a short knife-safety review. This unit's recipes call for diced onion and pepper, and the knife unit doesn't start until week 9.
steps: Fill a tall glass with ice, add cold water to just below the top of the ice, and stir. Let it stand 3 minutes.
Insert the probe at least 2 inches into the center of the glass, clear of the sides and bottom.
Wait for the reading to settle, about 30 seconds on a digital thermometer. It should read 32°F.

If it's more than 2°F off, recalibrate: most digital thermometers have a calibrate or reset function (see the manual); on a dial thermometer, an adult turns the nut under the dial with pliers until the needle reads 32°F. If it can't be adjusted, note the offset and correct for it every time.
Record readings for warm and cold tap water as well, so you get used to how quickly the probe settles.
Wash the probe in hot, soapy water. From now on, clean it after every use.
Knife review: set the cutting board on a damp paper towel so it can't slide. Grip the knife at the handle, and hold the food in a claw grip, fingertips curled under.
Halve an onion through the root, lay the halves flat side down, and chop them, moving your guide hand back with each cut. If the knife falls, step back and let it drop.
Use the onion in this week's recipe.

quiz.q: What should a calibrated thermometer read in ice water?
quiz.explain: An ice-water mixture stays at the freezing point of water, 32°F.

quiz.q: Why keep the probe away from the sides of the glass?
choices: The glass isn't the same temperature as the water
quiz.explain: You're measuring the water. The glass is warmer, so touching it skews the reading.

quiz.q: Your thermometer reads 35°F in ice water and can't be adjusted. A burger reads 162°F. What is it really?
quiz.explain: It reads 3°F high, so subtract 3. The burger needs another minute.

knowledge.title: Danger zone and how microorganisms grow
body: Most foodborne illness comes from microorganisms: bacteria such as Salmonella, E. coli, and Listeria, plus some viruses and parasites. They're common on raw meat, poultry, eggs, and produce, and you can't detect them by look, smell, or taste.

Bacteria multiply fastest between 40°F and 140°F, the range called the danger zone. Near body temperature, a population can double in as little as 20 minutes, so a few cells can become millions in a few hours.

Refrigeration (40°F or below) slows growth; freezing (0°F) stops it but doesn't kill anything. Cooking to a safe internal temperature kills most pathogens, and hot food held at 140°F or above stays out of the danger zone.

Some bacteria produce toxins that cooking doesn't break down, so reheating food that sat out too long doesn't make it safe. The USDA rule: cooked food goes into the fridge within 2 hours, or 1 hour when it's above 90°F.
steps: Leave your thermometer in a glass of water on the middle shelf of the fridge for an hour, then read it. Is the fridge at 40°F or below?
If you can, check the freezer the same way. Is it at 0°F or below?
If either runs warm, tell an adult. Turning the control a notch colder usually fixes it.

quiz.q: What is the danger zone?
quiz.explain: Bacteria multiply fastest in this range.

quiz.q: How long can cooked food stay at room temperature?
quiz.explain: After that, enough growth may have happened to make someone sick.

quiz.q: Why doesn't reheating rescue food that sat out all day?
choices: Some bacteria leave toxins that heat doesn't destroy
quiz.explain: Cooking kills the bacteria, but not every toxin they made.

sabbath.title: Label and date containers
body: Many families cook or prep ingredients ahead so they can spend the Sabbath resting instead of working in the kitchen. Food made ahead only helps if it's stored well, and this unit's Beyond the Recipe pages cover how: labeling, cooling, storing, and reheating.
Labels tell everyone what a container holds and when it was made, so nothing is eaten past its time or forgotten in the back.

The USDA guideline is 3 to 4 days in the fridge for cooked meat, poultry, soups, and stews. Many other leftovers keep longer, and hard-cooked eggs keep a week. Risk still climbs with time, because Listeria can grow at fridge temperatures and smell won't reveal it. Your family decides its own limits; the date on the label is what lets you apply them.
Frozen food stays safe indefinitely at 0°F, though it tastes best within 2 to 3 months.
steps: Put together a labeling kit: masking tape and a permanent marker, kept near the fridge.
Label every container from this week's cooking with the dish and the date it was cooked, for example "Shakshuka 10/4".
Go through the fridge with an adult and decide what's past your family's limit.
Move older food to the front so it gets used first.
Label anything you make ahead this week the moment it goes into the fridge.

quiz.q: What is the USDA guideline for cooked meat and poultry leftovers in the fridge?
quiz.explain: Other foods vary: many keep longer, and hard-cooked eggs keep a week.

quiz.q: Why can't you judge old leftovers by smell?
choices: The microorganisms that make food smell bad aren't the ones that make you sick
Smell only works on raw food
quiz.explain: Spoilage organisms cause smells and slime; pathogens like Listeria usually don't.

drill.title: Temp-check thick vs. thin patties
body: Patty thickness changes cooking time more than most people expect. Cook a thin and a thick patty side by side and track both with the thermometer.
You'll need an extra ½ pound of ground beef, or two of this week's patties.
steps: Split ½ pound of ground beef in two. Shape one patty about ¼ inch thick and one about ¾ inch thick.
Wash your hands and wipe down anything the raw beef touched.
Heat a skillet over medium-high with 1 teaspoon of oil until it shimmers. Add both patties with tongs, then wash the tongs and your hands.
When the undersides are browned, flip both and start a timer.
Check each patty from the side every minute after the flip, and record time and temperature.
Pull each patty when it reaches 160°F, and note its total time.
Compare the two. How much longer did the thick one take? Did either look done before it actually was?

quiz.q: Which patty takes longer to reach 160°F?
quiz.explain: Heat has farther to travel to the center.

quiz.q: A burger is brown all the way through. Is it done?
choices: Yes, if the juices run clear
quiz.explain: Ground beef can brown before it reaches a safe temperature, and can stay pink after it does. Color isn't reliable.

knowledge.title: Safe internal temperatures chart
body: The USDA publishes a minimum safe internal temperature for each kind of food, measured in the thickest part.

Poultry, whole or ground: 165°F. Ground beef and ground lamb: 160°F. Egg dishes: 160°F. Fish: 145°F. Leftovers and reheated food: 165°F. Whole cuts of beef and lamb (steaks, chops, roasts): 145°F with a 3-minute rest, which is medium.

Plenty of people eat steak rare (about 125°F) or medium-rare (about 135°F). For an intact whole cut, that's a much smaller risk than undercooking ground meat. Pathogens sit on the surface of a whole muscle, and a hard sear kills them, while the interior is close to sterile. Grinding spreads surface bacteria through the whole batch, which is why ground meat has to reach 160°F all the way through.

That reasoning only holds for intact cuts. It doesn't cover ground meat, poultry, or meat that has been needle-tenderized or injected with a marinade (the label will say so), and it doesn't cover anyone at higher risk: pregnant women, young children, older adults, or anyone with a weakened immune system.
For an accurate reading, put the tip in the thickest part, away from bone and the pan. With thin pieces, go in from the side, and check more than one piece.
steps: Make a temperature card: poultry 165°F, ground beef and lamb 160°F, eggs 160°F, fish 145°F, whole cuts 145°F (USDA), reheating 165°F.
Post it inside a cupboard door by the stove.

quiz.q: What temperature does ground turkey need to reach?
quiz.explain: All poultry, ground or whole, is 165°F.

quiz.q: Why is a rare steak lower risk than a rare burger?
choices: Grinding spreads surface bacteria through the meat; a steak's interior is nearly sterile
quiz.explain: Searing kills what's on a steak's surface. A burger's surface bacteria are mixed all the way through.

quiz.q: Which of these should never be served rare?
quiz.explain: Tenderizing pushes surface bacteria into the middle, so it needs the same care as ground meat.

sabbath.title: Cool a cooked dish in an ice bath
body: A large pot of hot food cools slowly, and its center can stay in the danger zone for hours, even in the fridge. It also warms everything stored around it.

The standard is two-stage cooling: from 140°F to 70°F within 2 hours, then to 40°F within 4 more. An ice bath handles the first stage; shallow containers, no more than 2 inches deep, handle the second.
steps: Pick something to cool: a pot of soup or rice, or a dish you're making ahead.
Fill the sink or a large bowl partway with ice and water.
Transfer the hot food to a metal bowl or pot and set it in the ice bath, with the water partway up the sides.
Stir every few minutes, and take the center temperature every 10 minutes. Record each reading.
At 70°F or below, divide it into shallow containers, cover, label, and refrigerate.
Note how long it took to go from 140°F to 70°F.

quiz.q: What is the time limit for cooling food from 140°F to 70°F?
quiz.explain: Then 4 more hours to reach 40°F.

quiz.q: Why do shallow containers cool faster than one deep one?
choices: The center is closer to the cold surface
quiz.explain: Less depth means heat has a shorter path out.

weeks.note: From the rice cooked and cooled in the drill

drill.title: Safe cooling of a batch of rice, saved for the fried rice
body: Cooked rice needs particular care. Raw rice often carries spores of Bacillus cereus, which survive cooking. If cooked rice sits warm, they grow and produce a toxin that reheating doesn't destroy. Cooled quickly and kept cold, rice is safe.
Do this the day before this week's fried rice. Fried rice works best with cold, day-old rice, so this batch goes straight into the recipe.
steps: Cook 2 cups of white rice in 3 cups of water: rinse, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on low until the water is absorbed.
Spread the hot rice in a thin layer on a sheet pan.
Let it cool uncovered until it stops steaming, about 20 minutes, then check the temperature in the middle of the layer.
Within 1 hour of cooking, and once it's below 70°F, pack it into a shallow container, cover, and label it.
Refrigerate it, and note the time from pot to fridge.
Use it in the fried rice within 1 to 2 days.

quiz.q: Why spread cooked rice on a sheet pan?
choices: A thin layer passes through the danger zone quickly
quiz.explain: More surface area means faster cooling.

quiz.q: Rice sat out warm all afternoon. What do you do?
quiz.explain: The Bacillus cereus toxin survives heat.

knowledge.title: Cross-contamination and board colors
body: Cross-contamination is the transfer of microorganisms from one food or surface to another, usually from raw meat to something that won't be cooked, by way of hands, knives, boards, or towels.

Commercial kitchens color-code cutting boards: red for raw meat, yellow for raw poultry, blue for raw fish, green for produce. At home, two boards cover it: one only for raw meat, poultry, and fish, and one for everything else.
With a single board, work from clean to raw: ready-to-eat foods and produce first, raw meat last, then wash the board, knife, and your hands in hot, soapy water.

Don't rinse raw poultry; it sprays bacteria around the sink and doesn't remove them. Cooked food goes on a clean plate, never the one that held it raw. Wash your hands after handling raw meat, eggs, or their packaging.
steps: Choose one cutting board for raw meat, poultry, and fish only, and mark it.
Go through this week's recipe and list every step that involves raw chicken or raw egg: what it touches, and where that gets washed.

quiz.q: With one cutting board, what order do you work in?
quiz.explain: Anything cut after raw meat on the same board picks up its bacteria.

quiz.q: Should you rinse raw chicken?
choices: No, it spreads bacteria without removing them
quiz.explain: Cooking to 165°F is what makes chicken safe.

quiz.q: The chicken is cooked. Where does it go?
choices: The plate it sat on raw
quiz.explain: Anything that held raw meat still carries its bacteria.

sabbath.title: Make a dish ahead and store it
body: This week puts the unit together: cook a dish ahead, cool it fast, and store it so it's safe and good when it's eaten. Many families do this before the Sabbath so they can rest; it works just as well for a busy weeknight.
Stored food stays out of the danger zone: cold at 40°F or below, or hot at 140°F or above if it's being held for a meal.
Braises like chicken adobo improve after a night in the fridge, which makes them good make-ahead choices.
steps: Pick a dish from this week to make ahead: the fried rice, chicken adobo, or something your family will eat later in the week.
Cook it a day or two before it's needed, and cool it quickly in shallow containers (week 2).
Cover and label it (week 1), and store it on a shelf, not in the door, which runs warmer.
Confirm the fridge is at 40°F or below.
If your family holds food hot for a meal, check that it stays at 140°F or above.

quiz.q: Where should make-ahead food be stored in the fridge?
quiz.explain: The door warms up every time it opens.

quiz.q: What temperature does hot-held food need to stay at?
quiz.explain: Below 140°F, it's in the danger zone.

weeks.note: Or beef kofta to 160°F, or turkey meatloaf to 165°F

drill.title: Set up a clean station unaided
body: Set up your own clean station without help. An adult checks it against the list but doesn't step in.
steps: Clear the counter of anything you won't use. Wash it with hot, soapy water and dry it.
Wash your hands with soap for at least 20 seconds.
Set out both cutting boards, raw-meat and general, each on a damp paper towel.
Set out a plate for raw meat, a separate plate for cooked food, and a bowl for scraps.
Calibrate the thermometer in ice water (week 1) and keep it within reach.
Fill one side of the sink or a dishpan with hot, soapy water for washing as you go.
Have the adult check your setup against this list, then cook this week's recipe from it.

quiz.q: How long should you wash your hands?
quiz.explain: That's the CDC guideline, with soap, scrubbing every surface.

quiz.q: Why two plates?
choices: One for raw meat, one for cooked food
quiz.explain: Cooked food never goes back on the raw plate.

knowledge.title: Food safety quiz
body: This quiz covers the whole unit. Answer from memory, then review anything you missed in weeks 1 to 3.

quiz.q: What is the danger zone?
quiz.explain: Bacteria multiply fastest in this range.

quiz.q: What temperature does chicken need to reach?
quiz.explain: All poultry, whole or ground.

quiz.q: What temperature does ground beef need to reach?
quiz.explain: Ground beef and ground lamb are 160°F.

quiz.q: Why can a steak be eaten rare when a burger can't?
choices: A steak's bacteria are on the surface, which the sear kills
quiz.explain: Grinding mixes surface bacteria through the whole patty.

quiz.q: What does a calibrated thermometer read in ice water?
quiz.explain: That's the reference point for checking it.

quiz.q: How long can cooked food sit out before refrigerating?
quiz.explain: After that, throw it out.

quiz.q: How do you cool a pot of soup quickly?
choices: Ice bath, stirring, then shallow containers
Put the whole pot in the fridge
Leave it on the stove overnight
quiz.explain: 140°F to 70°F within 2 hours, then 40°F within 4 more.

quiz.q: With one cutting board, what goes last?
quiz.explain: Then the board gets washed.

quiz.q: How hot should reheated leftovers get?
quiz.explain: Measured in the center.

quiz.q: What is the USDA guideline for cooked meat and poultry leftovers in the fridge?
quiz.explain: Many other leftovers keep longer, but risk still rises with time, because Listeria grows even in the fridge.

quiz.q: Rice sat out warm all afternoon. What do you do?
quiz.explain: Bacillus cereus toxin survives reheating.

sabbath.title: Reheat a stored dish to 165°F
body: Reheated leftovers need to reach 165°F at the center of the thickest piece. Warm to the touch isn't the same thing.
Reheat only what you'll eat. Each round of reheating and cooling costs quality and adds time in the danger zone.
steps: Choose a stored dish: this week's meatloaf, or something you made ahead.
Oven: portions in a baking dish with a splash of water or broth, covered with foil, at 350°F. Microwave: cover loosely, and stir or rotate every minute or two.
Check the center of the thickest piece. Keep heating until it reads 165°F.
Note the method and how long it took.
Serve it, or put it back in the fridge within 2 hours. Don't reheat the same portion twice.

quiz.q: Where do you check the temperature of reheated food?
choices: The center of the thickest piece
quiz.explain: The center heats last.

quiz.q: Why stir or rotate food in the microwave?
choices: Microwaves heat unevenly and leave cold spots
quiz.explain: A cold spot can still be in the danger zone.

recipes.title: Thick beef burgers

recipes.title: Sandwich loaf
recipes.skill: Kneading to a windowpane, baking a loaf
recipes.about: A soft white sandwich loaf, kneaded until the dough stretches thin, proofed in a loaf pan, and baked to 190°F inside.

recipes.title: Dinner rolls
recipes.about: Soft, buttery pull-apart rolls, each weighed so they bake evenly, with a cold overnight proof so they're ready to bake.

recipes.title: Tabbouleh
recipes.about: A bright parsley salad with mint, tomato, and a little bulgur, dressed with lemon and olive oil. The knife work is the dish.

recipes.title: Israeli salad
recipes.about: Cucumber, tomato, and pepper diced small and even, with parsley, lemon, and olive oil.

recipes.title: Garlic green beans
recipes.about: Green beans blanched bright green, then sautéed in shimmering oil with garlic until just blistered.

recipes.title: Beef picadillo
recipes.about: Ground beef browned over a sofrito of onion, pepper, and garlic, simmered with tomato, raisins, and olives, over rice.

recipes.title: Cajun rice dressing with beef
recipes.skill: An onion, celery, and pepper base, deglazing a pan
recipes.about: Louisiana rice dressing: ground beef browned with onion, celery, and bell pepper, the pan deglazed, and cooked rice stirred through.

recipes.title: Rice pilaf
recipes.about: Long-grain rice toasted in butter with a few broken noodles, then simmered in broth until every grain is separate.

recipes.title: Roasted vegetables
recipes.skill: Even cuts that roast at the same rate
recipes.about: A sheet pan of carrots, potatoes, peppers, and onion, cut so they roast evenly and brown at the edges.

recipes.title: Roast chicken pieces
recipes.about: Bone-in chicken thighs and breasts roasted with herbs until crisp, each checked with a thermometer: 165°F.

recipes.title: Baked fish with lemon and herbs
recipes.skill: Baking fish gently, checking pin bones
recipes.about: Salmon, cod, or tilapia fillets baked with lemon, dill, and garlic until they flake and reach 145°F, with a side timed to finish at the same time.

recipes.title: Steamed fish with ginger and scallion
recipes.about: White fish fillets steamed on a plate in a covered pot, then topped with ginger, green onion, soy, and a little warm oil.

recipes.title: Cod poached in tomato sauce
recipes.about: Cod fillets poached gently in a garlicky tomato sauce with olives and capers until they flake.

recipes.title: Pan-seared trout
recipes.about: Trout fillets seared skin-side down until the skin is crisp, finished with butter and lemon.

recipes.title: Vegetable stock
recipes.about: A clear stock from onion, carrot, celery, and herbs, simmered gently, skimmed, and strained, for soups later.

recipes.title: Chicken stock
recipes.about: The carcass from week 28's roast chicken, or chicken wings or backs, simmered slowly with vegetables, strained, cooled fast, and the fat lifted off.

recipes.title: Beef tacos with pico de gallo
recipes.skill: An even dice for pico de gallo
recipes.about: Seasoned ground beef browned to 160°F in warm tortillas, topped with a fresh pico de gallo of diced tomato, onion, jalapeño, and cilantro.

recipes.title: Kuku sabzi
recipes.skill: A big pile of finely chopped herbs
recipes.about: A Persian herb frittata: parsley, cilantro, dill, and green onion chopped fine, bound with eggs, and baked until set at 160°F.

recipes.title: Cuban black beans and rice
recipes.skill: Soaking and simmering dried black beans
recipes.about: Dried black beans soaked, simmered until creamy, and finished with a sofrito of onion, pepper, and garlic, over rice.

recipes.title: Bulgur pilaf with chickpeas
recipes.skill: Toasting bulgur, then cooking it by absorption
recipes.about: Coarse bulgur toasted in olive oil with onion and tomato paste, then simmered in broth with chickpeas until the liquid is gone.
